title: Selecting a PLL Architecture
intro: How to choose among the main PLL architectures for a team design: what each offers, a decision procedure from the specification, the simulations that confirm the choice, and the mistakes that most often sink one.

blocks.text: The candidates
1. Integer-N charge-pump PLL with an LC VCO

Tristate PFD, charge pump, passive second- or third-order filter, LC VCO with a capacitor bank, divider. The most mature and best-understood architecture; integrated jitter of roughly 100 to 500 fs is routine, reference spurs of $-60$ to $-80$ dBc with care. Frequency resolution equals $f_{ref}$, so a fine channel raster forces a low reference, a large $N$ and a narrow loop. Choose it for fixed-frequency clocks and coarse-raster synthesizers; it is the lowest-risk first design.
2. Fractional-N charge-pump PLL

The same blocks with a sigma-delta modulated divider, so $N$ may be fractional and the reference can be high. It adds quantization noise, which the loop must filter (pushing the loop narrower) or which must be cancelled; it makes PFD/CP linearity critical (offset pump or gated offset, matched pump) and adds fractional spurs. Choose it for RF synthesizers with fine channel spacing and for spread-spectrum clocks.
3. Charge-pump PLL with a ring VCO

Small and wide-range, but needs a wide loop to suppress the ring's noise, so a high reference frequency, and a clean regulated supply. Jitter typically one to a few picoseconds rms. Choose it for SoC and digital clocks where area matters more than jitter. Maneatis's self-biased loop keeps bandwidth proportional to frequency over a very wide range.
4. Sub-sampling (or sampling) PLL with an LC VCO

The reference samples the VCO directly, so in lock there is no divider and the detector noise is not multiplied by $N^2$. It gives the lowest in-band noise and jitter (tens of femtoseconds reported), but needs a frequency-locked loop for acquisition, attention to the sampler's kick-back spurs, and is integer-N unless a DTC is added. Choose it for very low-jitter clocks (high-speed links, data converters) when the team can absorb the extra design risk.
5. Digital PLL (TDC or bang-bang plus DCO)

A TDC or bang-bang detector, a digital loop filter and a digitally controlled oscillator (LC or ring). Small (no large capacitor), portable across nodes, easy to calibrate, reconfigure and test; in-band noise set by TDC resolution unless a DTC cancels the predictable part; limit cycles and DCO quantization need dithering. Choose it in fine-node SoCs and when the team is stronger in digital design and verification.
6. Injection-locked ring or multiplying DLL

A ring whose phase is reset by the reference every cycle. LC-like jitter at ring area, if the ring's free-running frequency is calibrated, otherwise reference spurs. Integer multiplication only. Choose it for multi-phase, low-area, low-jitter clocking when a clean, sharp reference is available.
A decision procedure

items: 1. Fix the specification: output range, channel step, reference available, phase-noise mask or jitter and its integration band, spurs, lock time, power, area, supply, process.
2. Channel step finer than any practical reference: fractional-N (or a digital PLL with fractional division).
3. Required VCO FoM (Choosing a VCO page): above about 165 dBc/Hz, LC (or injection-locked ring); below, a ring is possible if the loop can be wide.

4. In-band requirement: compute $\mathrm{FoM}_{1Hz} + 10\log f_{PFD} + 20\log N$ with a realistic $-220$ to $-230$ dBc/Hz pump. If that is too high, raise $f_{ref}$, consider a sub-sampling or sampling detector, or a fine TDC with DTC.
5. Loop bandwidth from the noise crossing, checked against $f_{ref}/10$, lock time and spur filtering (In-Band Noise widget, Loop Filter Design page).
6. Spur budget: estimate leakage and mismatch spurs (Charge-Pump Mismatch page) for the chosen $K_{VCO}$, $C_2$ and $f_{ref}$; choose the pump topology and filter order to meet it.
7. Risk and team: prefer the architecture whose difficult parts the team has done before and can verify with the tools it has.

blocks.text: Comparing the options at a glance

items: Jitter (typical): sub-sampling and DTC-assisted digital tens of fs; integer-N LC and fractional-N LC about 100 to 500 fs; injection-locked ring or MDLL a few hundred fs; ring CP-PLL one to several ps.
Area: ring-based and digital smallest; LC VCO plus a large filter capacitor largest.
Tuning range: rings widest; LC with banks 10 to 50%.
Spurs: integer-N with a matched pump best understood; sub-sampling and injection-locked designs need specific spur fixes; fractional-N adds fractional spurs.
Design and verification effort: integer-N lowest; fractional-N and sub-sampling add noise and spur modelling; digital PLLs need mixed-signal behavioural models and good DCO design.

blocks.text: Simulations that confirm a choice

items: Block noise: periodic steady-state (PSS) and periodic noise (Pnoise) for the VCO's phase noise and for the PFD/CP's output noise; transient noise as a cross-check.
Loop model: a phase-domain model (spreadsheet, Python or a PLL design tool) combining each block's noise with the loop response, swept over bands and corners.
Charge pump: $\Delta I/I_P$ against $V_{out}$ at all corners, Monte Carlo for random mismatch, transient charge per cycle in lock.
Closed loop: transient lock from start-up (including calibration) at each corner, phase margin and bandwidth across bands with $K_{VCO}$ and $N$ varying, spur levels from a long locked transient.
VCO: tuning curves and band overlap at all corners and temperatures, pushing, start-up margin (loop gain at least 2 to 3 at the worst corner), amplitude regime.

blocks.text: Mistakes that sink designs

items: A dead zone at the slow corner because the reset pulse was set at typical.
Pump mismatch checked only at mid-supply: the spur is far worse at the ends of the control range, which is where the extreme channels and temperatures put it.
Thin-oxide MOS capacitors in the loop filter in a leaky process, so leakage spurs dominate.
$K_{VCO}$ assumed constant: the loop is underdamped or unstable in the top band, sluggish in the bottom.
Bands that do not overlap at the hot or cold corner, leaving unreachable frequencies, or no margin for drift after calibration.
A ring VCO on a shared digital supply.
A loop bandwidth too close to $f_{ref}$ for the continuous-time model to hold.
Reference buffer with slow edges, whose noise becomes the in-band floor.

blocks.title: Team decision
blocks.text: Your team must deliver a 2.0 to 2.5 GHz synthesizer with 1 MHz channel steps from a 40 MHz crystal, $-115$ dBc/Hz at 1 MHz, reference spurs below $-65$ dBc, 5 mW total, in a 65 nm process. Which architecture, and what are the critical blocks?
solution: 1 MHz steps from 40 MHz need fractional-N (integer-N would need a 1 MHz reference, $N$ around 2250, and a loop narrower than 100 kHz).
VCO: $\mathrm{FoM}_{req} = 115 + 20\log_{10}2500 - 10\log_{10}P_{VCO}$; with about 2 mW for the VCO, $115 + 68.0 - 3.0 = 180$ dBc/Hz: a conventional LC core suffices, with a capacitor bank and AFC.
In-band: $-225 + 76.0 + 35.9 = -113$ dBc/Hz at $N = 62$; the loop must be narrow enough to filter sigma-delta noise but wide enough not to need a huge capacitor, a few hundred kHz.

Critical blocks: a linear PFD/CP for fractional-N (offset or gated offset, active current matching), low-leakage filter capacitors and a third pole for spurs, and $I_P$ programmed by band for $K_{VCO}$ variation.
blocks.answer: Fractional-N charge-pump PLL with an LC VCO; the critical block is a linear, well-matched charge pump.

blocks.title: When to take the risk
blocks.text: A team with one previous integer-N PLL tape-out is asked for a 10 GHz clock with under 60 fs rms jitter. Which architecture would you propose, and what would you do to manage the risk?
solution: 60 fs at 10 GHz is near the limit of good charge-pump designs; a sub-sampling PLL with a class-C or class-F LC VCO is the natural choice (Choosing a VCO, case C).

Manage the risk: keep a conventional PFD/CP frequency-locked loop as the acquisition path (it is also a fallback mode), model the sampler's kick-back early, and include test modes to measure the VCO free-running and each loop separately.
blocks.answer: A sub-sampling PLL with a high-FoM LC VCO, with a conventional loop kept as a fallback.
